Committed-use discounts (CUDs) and SUDs are mutually exclusive — resources covered by a CUD commitment are excluded from SUD calculations. SUDs are automatic, no-commitment savings; CUDs offer deeper discounts (37–55%) in exchange for a 1- or 3-year commitment.
words.connector: Think of sustained-use discounts like a coffee shop loyalty program that automatically punches your card: the more you visit in a month, the cheaper your next cup — no membership card to sign up for, no app to install.
words.techContext: Our always-on API servers receive the full SUD tier, effectively paying 30% less than on-demand pricing without any commitment — we verified this by comparing our billing report to the list price.
words.exampleSentence: After consolidating our workloads from 40 small N2 VMs to 15 larger ones in the same region, sustained-use discounts kicked in earlier each month, reducing our effective per-vCPU-hour rate by 18%.

codeExample.code:
# View current month's SUD credits in the billing export
# (Query in BigQuery against billing export dataset)
SELECT
  sku.description,
  SUM(cost) AS total_cost,
  SUM(credit.amount) AS sud_credit
FROM `billing_dataset.gcp_billing_export_v1_XXXXXX`
CROSS JOIN UNNEST(credits) AS credit
WHERE credit.type = 'SUSTAINED_USAGE_DISCOUNT'
  AND DATE(usage_start_time) >= DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), MONTH)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY sud_credit ASC

words.etymology: Sustained from Latin sustinere ('to hold up, to continue'); use referring to resource consumption; discount from Old French desconter ('to deduct'). The term was coined by GCP's billing team for this automatic savings mechanism.

words.shortDefinition: A GCP billing commitment offering 37–70% discounts in exchange for a 1- or 3-year pledge to consume a specific amount of compute resources.
words.simpleDefinition: Committed-use discounts (CUDs) are GCP's version of reserved instances — you commit to a minimum usage level for 1 or 3 years and receive a significant discount (up to 70% for 3-year GPU commitments) versus on-demand pricing. Two types exist: resource-based CUDs lock in a specific vCPU/memory amount; spend-based (flex) CUDs commit a dollar amount against any machine type in a family.
words.longDefinition: Committed-use discounts come in two variants optimized for different planning certainty levels. Resource-based CUDs commit to a specific vCPU count and memory amount within a machine family in a specific region for 1 or 3 years. They deliver the deepest discounts — 37% for 1-year and 55% for 3-year on general-purpose (N2, N2D, E2) families — and are the right choice for workloads with stable, predictable resource consumption. Spend-based (flex) CUDs commit to a minimum hourly dollar spend on a machine family in a region; they apply automatically to any machine type within that family, including custom machine types, at slightly lower discount rates (~28% for 1-year N2). Flex CUDs are the right choice when the specific machine type mix is expected to evolve. CUD coverage is measured at the project level in the Google Cloud Console's CUD analysis tool, which shows committed versus actual usage and waste. Commitments are binding — you are billed for the committed amount even if you run fewer resources. Model the steady-state baseline carefully, commit to that floor, and use on-demand or Spot VMs for burst capacity above the committed level. CUDs and sustained-use discounts (SUDs) do not stack — the hours covered by a CUD are excluded from SUD calculations.
words.connector: Think of a CUD like a gym membership: you pay a flat monthly fee for guaranteed access at a lower per-session rate. Resource CUDs lock you to specific equipment; flex CUDs let you use any machine in the family. Both save money only if you actually use what you commit to.
words.techContext: We purchase 3-year resource CUDs for our baseline compute (20 n2-standard-16 VMs) covering 55% savings, and use on-demand for burst capacity above that floor.
words.exampleSentence: The FinOps team's CUD analysis showed we were wasting 12% of our committed compute each month — consolidating workloads to fill the commitment before purchasing a larger one saved us $8,000/month.

codeExample.code:
# Purchase a 1-year resource-based CUD for N2 in us-central1
gcloud compute commitments create prod-n2-commitment \
  --plan 12-month \
  --region us-central1 \
  --resources vcpu=160,memory=640GB \
  --type GENERAL_PURPOSE_N2

# List existing commitments
gcloud compute commitments list --region us-central1

words.etymology: Committed from Latin committere ('to entrust, to pledge'); use referring to resource consumption; discount from Old French desconter. The pattern mirrors AWS Reserved Instances and Azure Reserved VM Instances.

words.shortDefinition: The GCP billing model where data transferred out of GCP — to the internet, to another region, or to another cloud — incurs per-GB charges, while data transferred in is free.
words.simpleDefinition: Egress pricing means GCP charges you for data leaving, not arriving. Data flowing out to the internet is most expensive; cross-region traffic within GCP is cheaper but non-zero; same-region, cross-zone traffic is cheapest but still billed. Egress is the surprise line item that first-time GCP bills reveal — architectures built without modeling data flows often exceed their compute budget on network costs alone.
words.longDefinition: GCP's egress pricing structure follows the physical economics of bandwidth: outbound traffic from Google's data centers has a real cost, while inbound traffic does not. The tier hierarchy from most to least expensive: internet egress (data leaving GCP to any public internet destination, billed per GB with a tiered rate that decreases at 1 TB, 10 TB thresholds, but never reaches zero); cross-region egress within GCP (traffic between GCP regions stays on Google's private backbone but is still billed — for example, a Cloud Run service in us-central1 calling a Cloud SQL instance in europe-west1); and cross-zone egress within a region (inter-zone traffic within the same region, the cheapest billed tier). Internet-free destinations exist: traffic between GCP services in the same region and same VPC is generally free — Cloud Run to Cloud SQL in the same region, Cloud Storage reads from GCE in the same region, and GKE pod-to-pod traffic within a cluster. Cloud CDN can dramatically reduce internet egress by serving cached responses from Google's edge, where each cache hit is billed at CDN egress rates (lower than standard internet egress). Cloud Interconnect and Cloud VPN also have data transfer pricing. FinOps teams consistently rank egress as the top surprise cost: model data flows during architecture design, place services that communicate frequently in the same region, and use Cloud CDN for public-facing content.
words.connector: Think of egress pricing like a hotel mini-bar: checking in is free, but every bottle you take out (data leaving GCP) has a price tag, and the further it travels from the hotel kitchen to your room, the higher the markup.
words.techContext: We co-located our image-processing Cloud Run service and Cloud Storage bucket in us-central1 to eliminate cross-region egress, saving $1,200/month on 3 TB/day of image data read from storage.
words.exampleSentence: Discovering that our CDN-bypass issue was routing 8 TB/month directly to the internet added $640/month to our bill — fixing the cache key configuration paid for the engineering time in two weeks.
words.etymology: Egress from Latin egressus ('a going out') — referring to data that exits the GCP network boundary; pricing from the commercial concept of setting a price for goods or services.
